<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The PKGBUILD's global/top-level scope contains only standard variable and array definitions: `pkgname`, `pkgdesc`, `pkgver`, `pkgrel`, `epoch`, `arch`, `url`, `license`, `depends`, `provides`, `conflicts`, `optdepends`, `options`, `source`, and `sha256sums`. There are no top-level command substitutions, no calls to `eval`, `curl`, `wget`, or any other commands that would execute during sourcing. No `pkgver()` function is present, and no code is embedded in the global scope outside of standard assignments. The `prepare()` and `package()` functions are defined but will not be executed by `makepkg --printsrcinfo`, so their contents are out of scope for this gate.

The source URL points to AMD's official ROCm repository (`stable.repo.amd.com`), which is the expected upstream for this package. A SHA256 checksum is provided.
</details>

<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This PKGBUILD packages AMD's ROCm Core SDK (RDNA4/gfx120X variant) as a binary distribution for Arch Linux. The source is downloaded from AMD's official repository at `stable.repo.amd.com`, which is the legitimate upstream distribution host. A SHA256 checksum is present, which pins the tarball content.

The `prepare()` function simply extracts the tarball using `bsdtar`, and the `package()` function performs standard packaging operations: moving extracted files into `$pkgdir`, creating symlinks (lib, include, bin → core equivalents), writing the OpenCL vendor ICD file, adding an `ld.so.conf.d` entry so the dynamic linker finds ROCm libraries, and writing a `profile.d` script that adds ROCm binaries to PATH. All of these are conventional steps for shipping a GPU/compute SDK.

There are no indicators of supply-chain attack: no obfuscated commands, no `eval`/`base64`/hex-encoded payloads, no `curl|bash` patterns, no `git pull` of mutable refs, no exfiltration of system data (e.g. `/etc/shadow`, SSH keys, environment variables) to remote hosts, and no unexpected file modification outside the package scope. The large `provides=`/`conflicts=` lists are typical for ROCm meta-packages that replace many split sub-packages.
</details>
<evidence>
</evidence>
<summary>
Standard ROCm binary AUR package with pinned upstream source.</summary>
</security_assessment>

The package downloads a single source tarball from `https://stable.repo.amd.com/rocm/core/tarball/therock-dist-linux-gfx120X-all-10.0.0.tar.gz`, which is AMD's official ROCm stable repository. The SHA256 checksum is properly pinned (`eb99db434a1738fd83b0c3b933146cdb76418f35fcf4647743fbdfef76e8c71f`), allowing verification of the downloaded artifact. The URL field uses plain HTTP (`http://www.amd.com`) but is only informational metadata, not used for downloads. The extensive list of `provides` and `conflicts` is typical of a meta-package bundling many ROCm components (hip, rocblas, miopen, rocfft, etc.), and the `options = !strip` is standard for binary packages.

No suspicious network requests, obfuscated content, or injected malicious code is present.
</details>
